items.content:
90% of a viral LinkedIn post depends on 1 thing.

Get it wrong, and the whole post could flop...

The hook determines whether people engage with your post or move on.

I've written hooks across 100s of accounts.

After 1,000+ posts tested across multiple brands, 
The formats winning 12 months ago aren't getting reach anymore.

In 2024, curiosity hooks dominated.
They were vague and clickbait-adjacent. 
"You won't believe what happened next" energy.

In 2026, authority hooks win.
And the algorithm prioritises content that gets read by the right people.

Your hook needs to do 2 things at once:
Stop the scroll, and signal who the post is for.

Here's the complete hook writing playbook for 2026:

1️⃣ How To

Lead with a powerful statement and drop the "how to" on line 2.

↳ Best for: Top of funnel reach and saves.
↳ Example: Delegation is the most underrated leadership skill. Here's how to do it properly:

2️⃣ How I

Lead with a specific result and a timeframe.

↳ Best for: Trust building and conversion content.
↳ Example: How I generated 23,000 leads in 30 days. Without running a single ad:

3️⃣ Contrarian

Make a strong, polarising claim.

↳ Best for: Reach, comments, and challenging bad advice.
↳ Example: Most LinkedIn advice is making your content worse. Here's what to do instead:

4️⃣ Shocking Stats

Lead with a number that stops the reader cold.

↳ Best for: Awareness content and broad reach.
↳ Example: 95% of LinkedIn posts get fewer than 1,000 impressions. Here's why yours is one of them:

5️⃣ Open Promise

Make a bold promise based on a credible result. Add a timeframe.

↳ Best for: Mid and bottom of funnel content.
↳ Example: This one change grew a LinkedIn account by 400% in 3 months. Here's exactly what changed:

Hook formats evolve, but the formatting rules never do:

Line 1: 62 characters maximum.
Line 2: 50 characters maximum.

No bold or italics in the hook, ever.
1 clear idea per hook.

Authority, specificity, and ICP relevance are doing more work in 2026 than shock alone.

Ask yourself this after every hook you write:
Would this stop me from scrolling?

If the answer isn't an immediate yes, rewrite it.

Hooks are the highest leverage skill on LinkedIn right now.
1 line can double your reach, or kill it entirely.

Start treating them like they matter that much.

items.content:
NOT every S&OP is equal.

This infographic shows immature vs mature S&OP:

Variability
↳ Immature: assumes a stable plan and reacts when it breaks
↳ Mature: builds plans expecting variability from the start

Forecast
↳ Immature: single numbers, example: “Forecast = 100K”
↳ Mature: ranges, example: “Forecast = 90–110K, here’s how we respond”

Constraints
↳ Immature: discovers bottlenecks when service drops
↳ Mature: knows what will break before it does

Trade-offs
↳ Immature: avoids difficult choices
↳ Mature: makes trade-offs visible; service vs inventory; cost vs responsiveness

Reaction to Noise
↳ Immature: adjusts plans constantly
↳ Mature: separates signal from noise and protects plan stability

Decisions
↳ Immature: waits for more data
↳ Mature: makes informed decisions with imperfect data

Alignment Before the Meeting
↳ Immature: uses S&OP to ‘figure things out’
↳ Mature: uses S&OP to confirm and commit

Any others to add?

Everyone tells you to "just post".

But nobody tells you the system for having a successful post.

That's why so many founders are stuck with flatlined reach, low engagement, and no leads, despite showing up every day.

They post, close the app... and nothing happens.

Their impressions drop, and comments dry up. 
So they start questioning whether LinkedIn even works.

It does, you just need the system around the post.

Here's the full system, broken into 3 parts :)

Part 1️⃣: Ideation
Don't start from scratch; use pre-validated content as your foundation.
Find what's already working in your niche, then make it yours 👇

→ Find a top-performing post in your space using Saywhat or Instagram.
→ Open Claude and drop it in as a reference.
→ Brief your angle: Same structure, your insight, your audience.
→ Review, refine, and hit publish.

Part 2️⃣: Going Live
Timing is a tactic, so use it.
Here's how to stop killing the post before it's even posted 👇

→ Post between 7–9 am or 12–2 pm in your audience's time zone.
→ Triple-check spelling and grammar before you go live.
→ Tag 1-2 relevant people max.

Part 3️⃣: After Posting
The next 30 minutes decide how far your content travels. 
This is where you can boost engagement with your ICP 👇

→ First 10 mins: Reply to every comment and engage on 5 posts.
→ Next 10 mins: Check if impressions are moving and profile visits are spiking.
→ Final 10 mins: Identify who engaged, and if they're in your ICP.

(Look for founders, operators, and decision-makers in the comments. 
These are the people worth engaging with directly.)

Most people post and close the app.
Don't be most people !

items.content:
Most plants don’t have a Lean problem.
They have a layer problem.

They try to improve culture before standard work exists.

They ask for accountability before the work is visible.

They install dashboards before people agree what “normal” looks like.

They run Kaizen events before daily management is stable.
And then everyone wonders why the improvement doesn’t hold.

A Lean operation is built in layers:

1. Standard work
2. isual management
3. Daily management
4. CI systems
5. Culture

Culture is NOT where you start.
Culture is what shows up after the lower layers become real on the floor.

If the standard is unclear, the board won’t save you.

If the board is ignored, the meeting won’t save you.

If the meeting has no action, the culture won’t change.

Start where the work happens.

Make the standard VISIBLE.

Then manage the gap every day.

That’s where Lean starts to hold.

What layer is weakest in most plants you’ve seen?

Most people think supply chains run on ERP systems 🖥

They don’t.

They run on a 3-layer 🌐planning engine.

And whether you manufacture products, distribute them, or simply procure and resell them…

the logic is fundamentally the same.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📊 LAYER 1 — DEMAND PLANNING
“What is likely to happen?”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

This layer senses and predicts demand using:

✅ Historical trends
✅ Promotions & pricing
✅ Market intelligence
✅ POS / downstream signals
✅ Seasonality
✅ AI-assisted forecasting
✅ Scenario planning

The goal is NOT perfect forecasting.

The real goal is:

⚡ Faster decision-making under uncertainty.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
⚙️ LAYER 2 — SUPPLY PLANNING
“How will the network respond?”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

This is the orchestration layer.

Depending on the business model, this may involve:

🏭 Manufacturing planning
📦 Inventory planning
🚚 Replenishment planning
🌐 Deployment planning
🛒 Allocation planning
🏢 Capacity planning

This layer balances:

⚖️ Service levels
⚖️ Capacity
⚖️ Inventory
⚖️ Lead times
⚖️ Cost
⚖️ Flexibility

This is where most supply chain trade-offs are made.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📦 LAYER 3 — EXECUTION PLANNING
“What exactly needs to happen?”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

This layer converts plans into execution:

✅ Purchase orders
✅ Supplier schedules
✅ Production orders
✅ Warehouse replenishments
✅ Transportation movements
✅ Inventory deployments

This is where instability gets amplified if upstream signals are weak.

And this is exactly why small demand changes often create massive upstream disruption.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🚨 WHY MANY PLANNING ORGANIZATIONS STILL STRUGGLE
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Because these layers often operate in silos.

Demand planners forecast.
Supply planners firefight.
Procurement expedites.
Warehouses react.
Finance questions inventory.

Everyone optimizes locally.
The network suffers globally.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🚀 WHAT LEADING ORGANIZATIONS ARE DOING DIFFERENTLY
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Modern supply chains are shifting toward:

✅ AI-assisted planning
✅ Real-time replanning
✅ End-to-end visibility
✅ Scenario simulations
✅ Constraint-aware planning
✅ Demand sensing
✅ Multi-echelon inventory optimization
✅ Integrated Business Planning (IBP)

The future of planning is no longer:

Forecast → Plan → Execute

It is becoming:

📡 Sense → Simulate → Decide → Adapt

Continuously.

And the companies that master this loop will build the fastest, smartest, and most resilient supply chains of the next decade.

But Very Few Truly Know Excel.

With 15+ years of Logistics & International Business experience, I’ve observed one clear pattern:
👉 Students understand concepts.
 👉 Professionals understand operations.
 ❌ But many struggle with Excel — the real backbone of supply chain decision-making.

Whether you are handling:
 • Inventory planning
 • Freight cost analysis
 • Lead time tracking
 • Demand forecasting
 • Supplier performance review
 • Safety stock calculation

Excel is not optional.
It is your silent competitive advantage.
Recently, I compiled a list of 50 Excel formulas that every Supply Chain & Logistics professional must know.

Not fancy formulas.
Not theoretical ones.

But formulas that are used daily in:
 ✔ Inventory sheets
 ✔ Freight comparison files
 ✔ MIS reports
 ✔ Forecast models
 ✔ KPI dashboards
 ✔ Purchase planning sheets

Here are a few examples:
 • SUMIFS() – Multi-condition cost analysis
 • XLOOKUP() – Faster and cleaner than VLOOKUP

 • DATEDIF() – Transit time calculation
 • NETWORKDAYS() – Working day calculation
 • FORECAST.LINEAR() – Demand projection
 • STDEV() – Safety stock support
 • IFERROR() – Clean reporting

Most professionals only use 5–6 formulas.
But mastering 30–40 of them can change how you analyze data forever.
